newsitem.title: INDIA: Saudi airline denounces mid-air collision reports.
newsitem.headline: Saudi airline denounces mid-air collision reports.

text.p: Saudi Arabian Airlines on Saturday denounced Indian newspaper reports suggesting its aircraft was responsible for the world's deadliest mid-air collision, in which 349 people died.

Several newspapers have said the flight recorder on the Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 cargo plane showed it was flying at the altitude set by air traffic controllers in New Delhi on November 12 when it collided with a Saudi jumbo jet.
The Times of India said on Saturday Kazakh investigators had concluded the crash was the Saudi pilots' fault.

The newspaper quoted Temirbulat Baisanov, head of the flight and navigation department of the company which owned the Kazakh plane, as saying the jet's flight recorders showed it was at the correct altitude.
The daily quoted Baisanov as telling the Russian news agency Interfax that the crew of the Saudi Boeing Co 747 jet "failed to perform a manoeuvre to avoid collision".

Saudi Arabian Airlines issued a statement saying it "denounced newspaper disclosures regarding alleged readouts from one of the flight recorders of the aircraft involved in the November 12 mid-air collision".
It said the reports were "either blatantly incorrect or a serious breach of official security in contravention of the letter and spirit of international law".

Several newspapers have said the Kazakh altimeter showed it was at or just below 15,000 feet (4,575 metres) when the Saudi airliner, which had been told by air traffic controllers to stay at 14,000 feet (4,270 metres), hit it.
The Times of India said Civil Aviation Ministry officials "now believed the Saudi plan could have been at fault".
The Saudi airline said it believed that neither of the flight recorders from the two aircraft had been decoded.

"If the recorder has actually been decoded at this stage, disclosure of the results could represent a blatant transgression of international law and the rights of all parties to the investigation," it said.

"But if the Kazakh recorder has not been read, then the so-called disclosure is blatantly incorrect, and could seriously jeopardise the integrity of the official inquiry," the statement quoted Captain Saad Al-Shehri, leader of the airline's support team assisting the investigation in New Delhi, as saying.
The Indian government has ordered a court of inquiry to complete its investigation by mid-February.

The Saudi airline said it had appealed to India's Director General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to issue a clarification that "so-called disclosures from nameless official sources are speculative, premature and liable to mislead the formal investigation".

"We reiterate our request that the DGCA take a firm position, stating clearly and publicly that all the evidence now being collected is in the secure custody of the official investigators," Al-Shehri said in the statement.

Earlier on Saturday, the Saudi airline reiterated an offer to pick up all "reasonable" funeral and related expenses incurred by the relatives of the 312 passengers on the Saudi jumbo jet who died in the accident.
All 37 passengers on the Kazakh plane died.
